course.title: Distributed Systems
course.description: How to build services that stay correct and available while spread across many machines that fail, lag, and disagree -- covering communication, time, replication, consensus, and the hard tradeoffs in between. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare 6.824 Distributed Systems (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The core reason distributed systems are hard is that...
options: machines and networks fail partially and independently
there are too many programming languages
questions.explanation: The defining difficulty is partial failure: some nodes and messages fail while others keep running, and you cannot always tell which -- see 'Why distributed systems'.

questions.prompt: A remote procedure call (RPC) tries to make a network request look like...
questions.explanation: RPC hides marshalling and network transport behind a normal-looking function call -- but the network can still fail, so the abstraction leaks.

questions.prompt: A Lamport logical clock guarantees that if event A causes event B, then...
options: A and B have equal timestamps
questions.explanation: Lamport clocks preserve the happens-before order: a cause always has a strictly smaller timestamp than its effect.

questions.prompt: Strong (linearizable) consistency means a read...
options: returns the result of the most recent completed write
is always faster than a weak read
questions.explanation: Linearizability makes the system behave as if there were a single, up-to-date copy: every read sees the latest completed write.

questions.prompt: The point of a consensus protocol like Raft is to get a group of nodes to...
options: agree on a single value or order of operations despite failures
questions.explanation: Consensus lets a replicated group agree on one outcome (such as the next log entry) even when some members crash -- see 'Consensus'.

questions.prompt: The CAP theorem says that when a network partition occurs, a system must give up...
questions.explanation: During a partition you can stay consistent (reject some requests) or stay available (risk stale answers), but not both.

questions.prompt: Two-phase commit (2PC) uses a prepare phase so that...
options: the coordinator can skip the commit
every participant votes before anyone commits, keeping the transaction atomic
questions.explanation: All participants must vote 'yes' in the prepare phase before the coordinator tells anyone to commit, so the transaction is all-or-nothing.

questions.prompt: Sharding (partitioning) a database primarily helps with...
options: making every node hold all data
spreading data and load across many nodes so the system scales
questions.explanation: Sharding splits the key space so each node owns a slice, letting total capacity and throughput grow with the number of nodes.

lessons.title: Why distributed systems: goals, failures, and the fallacies
lessons.grammar_note: In this course a 'node' is any single machine or process; a 'partition' means a network split that stops some nodes from reaching others (not a data shard -- context tells them apart).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why we accept the pain of distribution, name the ways a distributed system fails, and spot the classic false assumptions that sink naive designs. Warm-up: if a service runs on one machine and that machine dies, what fraction of your users are down?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: We distribute a system for three reasons: to scale beyond one machine's capacity, to tolerate failures so the whole service does not die when one part does, and sometimes to place data physically close to users. The price is that failures become partial and independent. A single machine mostly fails all-at-once -- it is up or it is down. A distributed system can have node 3 crashed, the link to node 5 dropping one message in ten, and node 7 running but paused for a slow garbage collection, all at the same time. Worse, a healthy node often cannot tell a crashed peer from a merely slow or unreachable one, because both look identical: no reply arrives. This is why the famous 'fallacies of distributed computing' are dangerous. They are the tempting but false assumptions that the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology never changes, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous. Every one of them is false in production, and each false assumption becomes a bug.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: a payment service on one server handles 1,000 requests per second, but traffic grows to 5,000. One machine cannot keep up, so you scale out to five nodes -- distribution for capacity. Scenario 2: an online store must not go fully dark when a server's power supply fails, so you run three replicas behind a load balancer -- distribution for fault tolerance. Scenario 3: a client calls a remote 'charge card' function and gets no response. Did the charge happen and the reply get lost, or did the server crash before charging? The client cannot tell from silence alone -- this ambiguity is the heart of partial failure, and it forces designs like idempotent retries. Scenario 4: a team assumes 'the network is reliable' and never handles a dropped message; the first packet loss during a sale corrupts an order. The fallacy became an outage.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three main reasons to build a distributed system. 2) From silence after a request, what two very different things might have happened? 3) Which fallacy does a design ignore if it assumes a call always returns instantly? 4) True or false: a slow node and a crashed node can look identical to a caller. 5) Give one concrete benefit of running three replicas instead of one. Answers: 1) scale/capacity, fault tolerance, and placing data near users. 2) the request succeeded but the reply was lost, or the server failed before doing the work. 3) 'latency is zero.' 4) True -- both produce no timely reply. 5) if one replica crashes, the other two keep serving, so the service stays up.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a timeout as proof that the work did not happen -- it may have happened with the reply lost, which is why retried operations should be idempotent. Mistake: designing only for total failure (all up or all down) and ignoring the messy partial states that actually dominate. Exit: (a) What makes distributed failure harder than single-machine failure? (b) Name any two fallacies of distributed computing. Answers: failures are partial and independent, and you often cannot distinguish crashed from slow; any two of -- the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology is static, one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous.

lessons.title: RPC and communication
lessons.grammar_note: 'At-least-once' means an operation may run more than once; 'at-most-once' means it runs zero or one time; 'exactly-once' is the ideal you approximate by combining retries with idempotency or deduplication.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how a remote procedure call works end to end, reason about what happens when a call fails, and choose the right delivery guarantee for an operation. Warm-up: if 'charge the card' might be retried after a lost reply, why is it dangerous to run it twice?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Nodes talk by passing messages, but writing raw socket code for every interaction is tedious, so we wrap it in remote procedure call (RPC): the client calls what looks like a normal function, a client stub marshals (serializes) the arguments into bytes, the bytes travel over the network, a server stub unmarshals them, runs the real function, and sends the result back the same way. The abstraction is convenient but leaky, because the network can drop, delay, duplicate, or reorder messages. That forces a choice of delivery semantics. At-least-once keeps retrying until it gets a reply, so the operation may execute more than once. At-most-once uses request IDs to detect and discard duplicates, so it runs zero or one time. True exactly-once is not directly achievable over a faulty network, so in practice you build it by making operations idempotent (running twice has the same effect as running once) or by deduplicating on a unique request ID. The rule of thumb: reads and idempotent writes are safe to retry; non-idempotent writes need a deduplication key.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: a client calls incrementCounter() and the network drops the reply. Under at-least-once it retries, so the counter jumps by 2 -- a bug, because increment is not idempotent. Scenario 2: the same call is redesigned as setCounter(id=req-91, value=5). Retrying with the same request ID is harmless because the server remembers it already applied req-91 -- at-most-once via deduplication. Scenario 3: a read getBalance() is retried freely; reading twice returns the same balance, so it is naturally idempotent. Scenario 4: a money transfer is made safe by giving each transfer a unique ID; the server records applied IDs, so a retried 'transfer req-204' is recognized and ignored rather than double-charging. Scenario 5: an RPC to a crashed server times out; the client cannot tell whether the work ran, so it must rely on the request ID to make a retry safe.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does the client stub do to the arguments before they hit the network? 2) Which delivery guarantee may run an operation more than once? 3) Why is getBalance() safe to retry without any special handling? 4) How do you make a non-idempotent write safe to retry? 5) Is 'append X to a log' idempotent if retried naively? Answers: 1) it marshals (serializes) them into bytes. 2) at-least-once. 3) it is idempotent -- reading twice yields the same value and changes nothing. 4) attach a unique request ID and have the server deduplicate, or redesign the operation to be idempotent. 5) no -- a naive retry appends X twice, so it needs a request ID or dedup key.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming RPC hides the network well enough that you can ignore failures -- the abstraction leaks, and every call can fail. Mistake: retrying a non-idempotent operation with no deduplication, which double-applies it whenever a reply is lost. Exit: (a) What is the difference between at-least-once and at-most-once? (b) Name one way to make a retried write safe. Answers: at-least-once may run an operation more than once while at-most-once runs it zero or one time; make the operation idempotent or deduplicate on a unique request ID.

lessons.title: Time and logical clocks: Lamport and vector clocks
lessons.grammar_note: 'Happens-before' is a partial order written A -> B: it holds if A and B are on the same node with A first, or A is a send and B is its receive, or by chaining those. If neither A -> B nor B -> A, the events are concurrent.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why wall-clock time is unreliable across machines, compute Lamport timestamps, and use vector clocks to tell whether two events are ordered or concurrent. Warm-up: two servers log an event at '10:00:00.000' by their own clocks -- can you trust that they truly happened at the same instant?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Physical clocks on different machines drift and are only loosely synchronized, so you cannot order events across nodes just by comparing wall-clock timestamps. Instead we track causality with logical clocks. A Lamport clock is one integer per node: increment it on every local event, attach it to every message you send, and on receiving a message set your clock to max(local, received) + 1. This guarantees that if A happens-before B then timestamp(A) is less than timestamp(B). The catch is the converse is not true -- a smaller timestamp does not prove causality, so Lamport clocks cannot detect concurrency. Vector clocks fix that. Each node keeps a vector with one counter per node; it increments its own entry on each event and, on receive, takes the element-wise maximum of its vector and the message's vector (then bumps its own entry). Compare two vectors element-wise: if every entry of V(A) is less than or equal to V(B) and at least one is strictly smaller, then A happens-before B; if neither dominates the other, the events are concurrent.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Lamport: node P does event a (clock 1) then sends a message stamped 2. Node Q, at clock 4, receives it and sets its clock to max(4, 2) + 1 = 5, so the receive has timestamp 5, safely greater than the send's 2 -- causality preserved. Vector clocks with nodes [P, Q]: P starts [0,0], does an event -> [1,0], sends stamped [1,0]. Q starts [0,0], does a local event -> [0,1], then receives P's message: max([0,1],[1,0]) = [1,1] then bump Q -> [1,2]. Now compare P's [1,0] with Q's earlier [0,1]: neither is less-than-or-equal to the other, so those two events are concurrent -- something a single Lamport number could never reveal. Compare [1,0] with [1,2]: every entry of [1,0] is at most [1,2] and one is smaller, so the first happens-before the second.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why can't you order cross-node events by wall-clock timestamps? 2) On receiving a message stamped 7 while your Lamport clock is 3, what is your new clock? 3) Does timestamp(A) < timestamp(B) under a Lamport clock prove A caused B? 4) Vectors [2,1] and [1,3]: ordered or concurrent? 5) Vectors [1,1] and [2,3]: which happened first? Answers: 1) physical clocks drift and are not perfectly synchronized. 2) max(3, 7) + 1 = 8. 3) no -- Lamport clocks cannot distinguish causality from coincidence, only guarantee the forward direction. 4) concurrent -- neither dominates ([2,1] wins position 0, [1,3] wins position 1). 5) [1,1] happens-before [2,3], since each entry of [1,1] is less than or equal to [2,3] and at least one is strictly smaller.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a Lamport ordering backwards -- a smaller timestamp does not imply causality, only that IF A -> B THEN timestamp(A) < timestamp(B). Mistake: forgetting to take the element-wise maximum on receive, which breaks the vector clock's ability to capture merged history. Exit: (a) What update does a Lamport clock do on receiving a message? (b) How do vector clocks show that two events are concurrent? Answers: set the clock to max(local, received) + 1; when neither vector is element-wise less than or equal to the other, so neither happened-before the other.

questions.prompt: A caller gets no reply after an RPC. This ambiguity is an example of...
questions.explanation: The work may have succeeded with a lost reply, or failed before running -- the caller cannot tell, which is partial failure.

questions.prompt: Which operation is naturally safe to retry with no deduplication?
questions.explanation: getBalance() is idempotent: reading twice returns the same value and changes nothing.

questions.prompt: At-least-once delivery means an operation may...
questions.explanation: At-least-once keeps retrying until it gets a reply, so the operation can execute multiple times.

questions.prompt: On receiving a message stamped 6 while its Lamport clock is 9, a node sets its clock to...
Vector clocks [3,1] and [1,2] are...
questions.explanation: Neither vector is element-wise less than or equal to the other, so the events are concurrent.

questions.prompt: The assumption 'the network is reliable' is best described as...
options: one of the fallacies of distributed computing
questions.explanation: It is a classic fallacy -- false in production, and each such false assumption turns into a bug.

lessons.title: Replication and consistency models
lessons.grammar_note: 'Consistency' here means how up-to-date and agreeing the replicas look to clients (linearizable, causal, eventual) -- a different meaning from the 'C' of ACID transactions, which is about honoring database invariants.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why we replicate data, distinguish strong from eventual consistency, and pick a model given an application's needs. Warm-up: if you keep three copies of a value and a client writes to one, what should another client reading a different copy see?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Replication means keeping multiple copies of data on different nodes, for fault tolerance (survive a copy dying), for read throughput (many replicas answer reads), and for locality (a copy near the user). The hard question is what a client is allowed to observe when copies can disagree temporarily. A consistency model is the contract. Linearizable (strong) consistency makes the system behave as if there is a single copy updated instantly: every read returns the most recent completed write, and once one client sees a new value, no one later sees an older one. Causal consistency is weaker: operations that are causally related are seen by everyone in the same order, but unrelated operations may be seen in different orders. Eventual consistency is weakest: if writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value, but in the meantime reads can be stale. Stronger models are easier to program against but cost more coordination and latency; weaker models are faster and more available but push correctness work onto the application.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: a bank balance must be linearizable -- after you deposit and see the new balance, no later read anywhere may show the old one, or you could overdraw. Scenario 2: a social feed is fine with eventual consistency -- if a friend in Tokyo sees your post a second later than a friend nearby, nothing breaks. Scenario 3: causal consistency matters for a comment thread: everyone must see a reply after the message it answers (the cause before the effect), even if two unrelated top-level posts appear in different orders on different screens. Scenario 4: a shopping cart uses eventual consistency and briefly shows a just-removed item on one device; it converges within a second, which is acceptable. Scenario 5: choosing linearizable for a feature that does not need it (like view counts) needlessly adds coordination latency to every read.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Give three reasons to replicate data. 2) Under linearizable consistency, what does every read return? 3) Which model only promises that replicas converge once writes stop? 4) Which model guarantees a reply is never seen before the message it answers? 5) What is the cost of choosing a stronger model than you need? Answers: 1) fault tolerance, higher read throughput, and locality (a copy near users). 2) the most recent completed write. 3) eventual consistency. 4) causal consistency. 5) extra coordination and higher latency for no benefit.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming replication automatically gives strong consistency -- copies disagree unless a protocol keeps them in step, and that protocol costs latency. Mistake: reaching for linearizable everywhere when eventual consistency would be cheaper and perfectly acceptable. Exit: (a) What does eventual consistency promise, and what does it not promise? (b) Why is a bank balance a poor fit for eventual consistency? Answers: it promises replicas converge to the same value once writes stop, but not that reads are fresh in the meantime; a stale balance read could let a client overdraw, so it needs linearizable reads.

lessons.title: Consensus: the problem and Paxos/Raft intuition
lessons.grammar_note: A 'majority' (quorum) of a group of N nodes is any subset of more than N/2 of them. Any two majorities overlap in at least one node -- the key fact that keeps consensus safe.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the consensus problem and its safety and liveness goals, and explain at an intuitive level how a leader-based protocol like Raft reaches agreement despite failures. Warm-up: why does requiring a majority to agree, rather than everyone, let the system make progress when one node is down?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Consensus is the problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value -- most usefully, the next entry in a shared log of operations -- even though nodes can crash and messages can be lost or delayed. A good protocol must be safe (never two nodes deciding different values) and, when the network is behaving, live (it eventually decides). The trick that makes both possible is the majority quorum: any decision needs votes from more than half the nodes, and because any two majorities share at least one node, two conflicting decisions can never both gather a majority. Raft makes this understandable with a leader. Time is divided into numbered terms; in each term nodes elect one leader by majority vote. Clients send commands to the leader, which appends them to its log and replicates them to followers. Once a majority has stored an entry, the leader marks it committed and applies it, safe in the knowledge it can never be lost. If the leader crashes, followers notice the missing heartbeats, a new term begins, and a node with an up-to-date log wins the next election. Paxos reaches the same guarantees through a more abstract prepare-and-accept exchange, but the intuition -- majorities that must overlap -- is identical.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: a 5-node Raft cluster needs 3 votes for anything. Two nodes crash; the remaining 3 still form a majority, so the cluster keeps committing entries. A third crash leaves only 2, no majority, so it safely stops rather than risk splitting. Scenario 2: a network partition splits 5 nodes into a group of 3 and a group of 2. Only the side with 3 can elect a leader and commit; the minority side cannot, which prevents two leaders from accepting conflicting writes -- no split brain. Scenario 3: a leader appends 'set x=7', replicates it to 2 followers (3 of 5 total have it), and commits; even if the leader dies immediately after, any new leader must be elected by a majority that includes a node holding x=7, so the entry survives. Scenario 4: two candidates split the vote in a term and neither gets a majority; after randomized timeouts one retries first, wins the next term, and progress resumes -- liveness restored without ever violating safety.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What single thing does consensus get nodes to agree on, in the log-based framing? 2) In a 7-node cluster, how many nodes form a majority? 3) Why can a 5-node cluster keep working after 2 crashes but not after 3? 4) During a partition into groups of 3 and 2, which side can commit, and why does that prevent split brain? 5) What guarantees a committed entry survives a leader crash? Answers: 1) the next entry (and thus the order of operations) in a shared log. 2) 4 (more than half of 7). 3) 2 failures leave 3 of 5, still a majority; 3 failures leave 2, which is not a majority, so it halts to stay safe. 4) the side with 3 (a majority) can elect a leader and commit; the side with 2 cannot, so only one side ever accepts writes. 5) any new leader is chosen by a majority, which must overlap the majority that stored the entry, so at least one elector holds it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking consensus needs every node to agree -- it needs a majority, which is exactly what lets it tolerate a minority of failures. Mistake: assuming a partitioned minority can keep serving writes; it cannot commit, precisely to avoid two leaders diverging. Exit: (a) Why can two conflicting values never both be decided? (b) What is the minimum number of live nodes for a 5-node cluster to make progress? Answers: any decision needs a majority and any two majorities overlap in at least one node, so they cannot both be gathered for conflicting values; 3 live nodes (a majority of 5).

lessons.title: Fault tolerance and replicated state machines
lessons.grammar_note: A 'deterministic' operation produces the same result and same state change every time it runs on the same input and prior state -- no randomness, no reading the wall clock, no unsynchronized external calls.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the replicated state machine approach to fault tolerance and why every replica must apply the same operations in the same order to stay identical. Warm-up: if two copies of a service start identical and then each applies the same list of commands in the same order, how do their final states compare?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The dominant recipe for a fault-tolerant service is the replicated state machine (RSM). Model your service as a state machine: it has some state and a set of deterministic operations that move it from one state to the next. If you start several replicas in the same initial state and feed them the exact same sequence of operations, they will pass through the exact same states and stay identical -- so any surviving replica can serve the correct answer. The whole problem then reduces to agreeing on one ordered log of operations, which is exactly what consensus provides. A consensus protocol like Raft orders client commands into a replicated log; each replica applies committed log entries in order to its copy of the state machine. Two conditions make this work: operations must be deterministic (no randomness or reading the local clock, which would make replicas diverge), and every replica must apply entries in the identical committed order. If a replica falls behind or restarts, it catches up by replaying the log from a snapshot forward.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: three replicas of a key-value store each start empty and apply the same log -- put(a,1), put(b,2), put(a,3) -- so all three end with a=3, b=2 and any of them can answer a read correctly. Scenario 2: one replica crashes and restarts; it loads the latest snapshot, replays the log entries recorded after it, and rejoins fully caught up. Scenario 3: an operation calls random() to pick a value; replica 1 gets 4 and replica 2 gets 9, so their states diverge -- the fix is to compute the random value once, in the leader, and record the chosen number in the log so every replica applies the same value. Scenario 4: a replica applies log entry 12 before entry 11 by mistake; its state now differs from its peers -- a correctness bug caused by violating the same-order rule. Scenario 5: reading the local wall clock inside an operation makes replicas disagree; instead the leader stamps the time and stores it in the log entry.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what is the replicated state machine idea? 2) What two conditions keep replicas identical? 3) Why is calling random() inside an operation a problem, and how do you fix it? 4) How does a restarted replica catch up efficiently? 5) What subsystem provides the single agreed order of operations? Answers: 1) run identical deterministic state machines that apply the same operations in the same order, so surviving replicas stay correct. 2) operations are deterministic, and every replica applies committed entries in the identical order. 3) each replica would draw a different value and diverge; fix it by choosing the value once in the leader and recording it in the log. 4) it loads a snapshot and replays only the log entries after it. 5) a consensus protocol such as Raft, which produces the ordered replicated log.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: letting nondeterminism (randomness, wall-clock reads, unsynchronized external calls) leak into an operation, which silently makes replicas diverge. Mistake: assuming replicas can apply committed entries in any order they like -- the order must be identical everywhere. Exit: (a) Why must operations be deterministic? (b) What does consensus contribute to the RSM design? Answers: so that identical starting replicas fed identical inputs reach identical states; consensus supplies the single agreed order of operations in the replicated log.

questions.prompt: A bank balance is best served with which consistency model?
questions.explanation: A stale balance could let a client overdraw, so reads must be linearizable (strong).

questions.prompt: In a 5-node Raft cluster, how many nodes must store an entry before it is committed?
questions.explanation: A majority of 5 is 3; any two majorities overlap, which keeps the entry safe.

questions.prompt: During a partition of 5 nodes into groups of 3 and 2, which side can commit writes?
questions.explanation: Only the majority side (3) can elect a leader and commit, preventing split brain.

questions.prompt: For a replicated state machine to keep replicas identical, operations must be...
options: deterministic and applied in the same order
questions.explanation: Identical replicas fed identical, deterministic operations in the same order reach identical states.

questions.prompt: Causal consistency guarantees that everyone sees...
options: all operations in the same order
a reply only after the message it answers
the freshest value on every read
questions.explanation: Causally related operations (cause before effect) are seen in the same order by all; unrelated ones may differ.

questions.prompt: Calling random() inside a replicated operation causes...
questions.explanation: Each replica would draw a different value, so states diverge; the leader must fix the value in the log.

lessons.title: The CAP theorem and its tradeoffs
lessons.grammar_note: CAP's three letters are Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request gets a non-error response), and Partition tolerance (the system keeps working despite dropped messages between nodes). The theorem is about the choice forced during a partition.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the CAP theorem precisely, explain why partition tolerance is not optional, and classify real systems by the choice they make during a partition. Warm-up: if two halves of your cluster cannot talk and a client writes to one half, what should the other half do when a different client reads?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The CAP theorem says that when a network partition splits a distributed system so that some nodes cannot reach others, the system must choose between consistency and availability -- it cannot have both during the partition. Consistency here means every read returns the latest write (linearizable); availability means every request receives a non-error response. Partition tolerance is not really a choice: networks drop and delay messages, so any real distributed system must tolerate partitions. That leaves the genuine decision for partition time. A CP system keeps consistency by refusing requests it cannot safely serve -- it sacrifices availability, returning errors or timing out on the minority side rather than risk a stale answer. An AP system keeps availability by answering from whatever copy it has -- it sacrifices consistency, possibly returning stale data that reconciles later. The subtlety: when there is no partition, a well-built system can be both consistent and available; CAP only bites during the split. A related idea, PACELC, adds that even without a partition you trade latency against consistency.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: a Raft-backed configuration store partitions into 3 and 2 nodes. The minority side returns errors instead of possibly stale config -- a CP choice, favoring consistency over availability. Scenario 2: a shopping-cart service under partition still accepts add-to-cart on both sides and merges the carts afterward -- an AP choice, favoring availability, tolerating temporary divergence. Scenario 3: a leaderless quorum store is told to require reads and writes to touch a majority; during a 3-versus-2 split the minority cannot form a quorum and returns errors -- CP behavior emerges from the quorum rule. Scenario 4: a DNS-like system answers every query from a local cache even when cut off from the source, accepting brief staleness -- AP by design. Scenario 5: with no partition at all, the same Raft store serves reads quickly and consistently, showing that CAP's tradeoff is specifically a partition-time phenomenon.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What three properties do C, A, and P stand for? 2) Why is partition tolerance not really optional? 3) During a partition, what does a CP system give up, and how? 4) What does an AP system return during a partition, and what must it do later? 5) Is a system forced to choose between C and A when there is no partition? Answers: 1) Consistency (reads see the latest write), Availability (every request gets a non-error response), Partition tolerance (keeps working despite dropped inter-node messages). 2) real networks inevitably drop and delay messages, so the system must cope with partitions. 3) availability -- it returns errors or times out on the side it cannot safely serve. 4) possibly stale data, and it must reconcile or merge the divergent copies once the partition heals. 5) no -- CAP's tradeoff applies during a partition; without one a system can be both consistent and available (latency aside).

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading CAP as 'pick two of three' in general -- P is mandatory, so the real choice is C versus A, and only during a partition. Mistake: believing a system must always be either consistent or available; outside partitions it can be both. Exit: (a) During a partition, what is the actual choice CAP forces? (b) Give one example each of a CP and an AP choice. Answers: consistency versus availability; CP -- a Raft config store that errors on the minority side; AP -- a shopping cart that keeps accepting writes on both sides and merges later.

lessons.title: Distributed transactions and two-phase commit
lessons.grammar_note: 'Atomic' means all-or-nothing: either every participant applies the change or none does. A transaction that spans multiple nodes is atomic only if they agree to commit together.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why a single transaction across multiple nodes needs a commit protocol, walk through two-phase commit (2PC), and name its failure weakness. Warm-up: to move $100 from an account on node A to an account on node B, why is it unsafe for A to commit its debit before knowing B will commit the credit?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sometimes one logical transaction touches data on several nodes -- debit here, credit there -- and it must be atomic: all the parts commit or none do, or you get lost money and broken invariants. Two-phase commit (2PC) coordinates this. A coordinator drives two rounds among the participants. Phase 1, prepare: the coordinator asks every participant 'can you commit this?' Each participant does the work tentatively, writes it to durable storage, locks the affected data, and votes yes only if it is certain it could commit; otherwise it votes no. Phase 2, commit or abort: if every vote was yes, the coordinator records a commit decision and tells all participants to commit; if any voted no (or timed out), it tells everyone to abort. Because a participant that voted yes has durably promised, it must be able to commit even after a crash-and-restart. 2PC gives atomicity, but it has a serious flaw: it is a blocking protocol. If the coordinator crashes after participants have voted yes but before delivering the decision, those participants are stuck holding locks, unable to safely commit or abort on their own, until the coordinator recovers. Production systems mitigate this by making the coordinator itself fault-tolerant (for example, replicated via consensus).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: transfer $100 from A to B. Prepare: A tentatively debits and locks the account, B tentatively credits and locks, both vote yes. Commit: the coordinator says commit, both make it permanent and release locks -- atomic transfer. Scenario 2: during prepare, B has insufficient-funds rules violated and votes no; the coordinator tells both to abort, A rolls back its tentative debit, and no money is lost. Scenario 3: the coordinator crashes right after collecting two yes votes but before sending the decision; A and B sit locked and blocked, waiting -- the classic 2PC stall -- until the coordinator recovers its decision log and finishes. Scenario 4: to reduce that risk, the coordinator's decision is itself stored in a Raft group, so a coordinator replica can take over and deliver the outcome. Scenario 5: a participant that voted yes crashes and restarts; because it durably logged its tentative change, it can still honor the commit when the decision arrives.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What property must a multi-node transaction have, and what does it mean? 2) What does a participant do during the prepare phase before voting yes? 3) What happens in phase 2 if even one participant votes no? 4) Why is 2PC called a blocking protocol? 5) How do production systems reduce 2PC's coordinator weakness? Answers: 1) atomicity -- all participants apply the change or none do. 2) it does the work tentatively, writes it durably, locks the data, and votes yes only if certain it can commit. 3) the coordinator tells everyone to abort, and all participants roll back. 4) if the coordinator crashes after yes votes but before the decision, participants are stuck holding locks, unable to safely decide alone. 5) by making the coordinator fault-tolerant, for example replicating its decision via a consensus group so another replica can finish.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: letting a participant commit its part before the coordinator's decision -- that breaks atomicity if another participant aborts. Mistake: assuming 2PC is fully fault-tolerant; a coordinator crash at the wrong moment blocks participants until recovery. Exit: (a) What does a yes vote in phase 1 promise? (b) What is 2PC's main weakness? Answers: that the participant has durably prepared and can commit when told, even after a restart; it blocks -- a coordinator failure between voting and decision leaves participants stuck holding locks.

lessons.title: Sharding and partitioning
lessons.grammar_note: Beware overloaded words: 'partition' in this lesson means a shard (a slice of the data assigned to a node), whereas in the CAP and failure lessons 'partition' meant a network split. The surrounding topic tells you which is meant.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why we shard data across nodes, compare range and hash partitioning, and recognize and avoid hot spots. Warm-up: if one database node can hold 100 GB but you have 1 TB of data, how many nodes do you need, and how should you decide which key goes where?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When data or load outgrows one node, you shard (partition) it: split the key space into pieces and assign each piece to a different node, so total capacity and throughput grow with the number of nodes. The central design choice is the partitioning function -- how a key maps to a shard. Range partitioning assigns contiguous key ranges (A-F on node 1, G-M on node 2, and so on); it makes range scans efficient but risks hot spots when many requests cluster in one range. Hash partitioning applies a hash to the key and uses that to pick a shard; it spreads load evenly and avoids most hot spots, but scatters range scans across many nodes. A hot spot is a single shard receiving a disproportionate share of traffic -- for example, all writes landing on the newest key range, or one celebrity account overwhelming its shard. To keep balance as the cluster changes, systems use consistent hashing, which places nodes and keys on a ring so that adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys rather than reshuffling everything. Rebalancing shards as nodes join and leave is an ongoing operational job, not a one-time setup.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: 1 TB of data on nodes that hold 100 GB each needs at least 10 shards spread across 10 nodes. Scenario 2: range partitioning by timestamp puts all of today's writes on the newest range, so one node is hammered while others idle -- a hot spot; switching to hash partitioning on the key spreads those writes evenly. Scenario 3: a shop needs to list all orders from June; under range partitioning by date those sit on one shard (a fast scan), but under hash partitioning they are scattered across every shard (slower) -- a real tradeoff. Scenario 4: a viral celebrity account concentrates traffic on its shard; the fix is to split that hot key further or replicate it for reads. Scenario 5: adding an 11th node under consistent hashing moves only about one-eleventh of the keys, so rebalancing is cheap; naive modulo hashing would remap almost everything.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why do we shard data across nodes? 2) Which partitioning scheme makes range scans efficient but risks hot spots? 3) Which scheme spreads load evenly but scatters range scans? 4) What is a hot spot, and give one cause. 5) What problem does consistent hashing solve when a node is added? Answers: 1) so total capacity and throughput scale with the number of nodes, beyond what one node can hold or serve. 2) range partitioning. 3) hash partitioning. 4) a shard taking a disproportionate share of traffic -- caused, for example, by all new writes landing on the newest range or one celebrity key. 5) it moves only a small fraction of keys, avoiding a full reshuffle of the data.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: partitioning by a monotonically increasing key (like a timestamp) and sending every new write to the same shard -- an instant hot spot. Mistake: assuming hash partitioning is always best; it makes range queries scan every shard. Exit: (a) What is the difference between range and hash partitioning? (b) Why is consistent hashing preferred when the cluster size changes? Answers: range keeps contiguous key ranges together (good scans, hot-spot risk) while hash scatters keys evenly (balanced load, scattered scans); consistent hashing remaps only a small fraction of keys when a node joins or leaves, instead of nearly all of them.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, the CAP theorem forces a choice between...
questions.explanation: Partition tolerance is mandatory, so the real choice during a partition is consistency versus availability.

questions.prompt: In two-phase commit, a participant that votes yes in the prepare phase has...
options: durably promised it can commit when told
questions.explanation: A yes vote is a durable promise: the participant must be able to commit later, even after a crash and restart.

questions.prompt: The main weakness of two-phase commit is that it...
options: blocks if the coordinator crashes at the wrong moment
questions.explanation: If the coordinator fails after yes votes but before the decision, participants are stuck holding locks until it recovers.

questions.prompt: Partitioning by a monotonically increasing timestamp key tends to create...
options: a hot spot on the newest range
questions.explanation: All new writes land on the same newest range, overloading one shard -- a hot spot.

questions.prompt: Consistent hashing is valuable because when a node is added it...
options: moves only a small fraction of keys
questions.explanation: It moves only a small fraction of keys, avoiding a full reshuffle when the cluster changes size.

questions.prompt: An AP system, during a partition, will...
options: answer from whatever copy it has, risking stale data
questions.explanation: AP favors availability: it serves from an available copy and reconciles divergence after the partition heals.

lessons.title: Worked design: a fault-tolerant key-value store
lessons.grammar_note: This lesson assembles earlier pieces: a replicated log (consensus) for ordering, a replicated state machine for the data, request IDs for at-most-once semantics, and sharding for scale. Notice how each earlier concept plugs into one system.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace the full path of a request through a replicated, sharded key-value store and see how consensus, the replicated state machine, deduplication, and sharding fit together. Warm-up: which earlier subsystem gives every replica the same order of operations?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: We want a key-value store that survives node failures and scales past one machine. Design it in layers. Sharding: split the key space into shards, each owned by a replica group; hash partitioning spreads load and avoids hot spots. Replication and consensus: run each shard as a small Raft group (say 3 or 5 nodes) that keeps a replicated log; the group's leader accepts writes and replicates each command to a majority before committing. Replicated state machine: each replica applies committed log entries in order to its in-memory map, so all replicas of a shard hold identical data and any of them can be promoted if the leader dies. At-most-once semantics: clients tag each write with a unique request ID; the state machine records applied IDs so a retried write after a lost reply is deduplicated rather than applied twice. Consistency: because reads are answered by the leader from the committed state, clients get linearizable results. Put together: a client hashes the key to find the shard, sends the request (with its ID) to that shard's leader, the leader commits it through Raft to a majority, every replica applies it deterministically, and the leader replies. Failures are absorbed layer by layer -- a crashed follower is caught up by log replay, a crashed leader is replaced by a majority election, and a lost reply is made safe by the request ID.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Scenario 1: put(key='user:42', value='Ana', id=req-88). The client hashes 'user:42' to shard 2, sends to shard 2's leader, which appends the entry and replicates it to a majority of its Raft group; once committed, all replicas set user:42 = Ana and the leader acks. Scenario 2: the ack is lost and the client retries req-88; the leader sees req-88 already applied and returns the stored result instead of writing 'Ana' twice -- at-most-once in action. Scenario 3: shard 2's leader crashes mid-operation; its followers miss heartbeats, hold an election, and a follower with the latest log becomes leader, having already stored the committed entries -- no data lost. Scenario 4: traffic on shard 5 spikes because of one hot key; operators split that shard's range or add read replicas to relieve it. Scenario 5: a follower that was offline restarts, loads its snapshot, replays the committed log entries it missed, and rejoins as a full replica.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How does a client know which shard a key belongs to? 2) What role does Raft play inside each shard? 3) How does the design prevent a retried write from applying twice? 4) When a shard's leader crashes, how does the shard keep serving? 5) Why can any replica of a shard answer correctly for that shard? Answers: 1) it hashes the key to map it to a shard. 2) it maintains the replicated log and commits each write to a majority, providing a single agreed order of operations. 3) each write carries a unique request ID and the state machine deduplicates already-applied IDs. 4) the followers hold a majority election and a node with the up-to-date log becomes the new leader. 5) all replicas apply the same committed operations in the same order, so they hold identical state.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: skipping request IDs and assuming retries are harmless -- without deduplication a lost reply leads to a double write. Mistake: letting a partitioned minority of a shard's Raft group keep serving writes; only the majority side may commit. Exit: (a) Name the four subsystems this design combines. (b) What single earlier concept guarantees all replicas of a shard stay identical? Answers: sharding, consensus (a replicated log via Raft), the replicated state machine, and at-most-once via request IDs; applying the same committed operations in the same deterministic order (the replicated state machine backed by consensus).

questions.prompt: The single hardest feature of distributed systems, versus single machines, is...
options: partial and independent failure you often cannot diagnose
questions.explanation: Parts fail independently and a crashed node can look identical to a slow one -- partial failure is the core difficulty.

questions.prompt: You must retry a non-idempotent write safely. The standard technique is to...
options: attach a unique request ID and deduplicate on the server
questions.explanation: A request ID lets the server recognize and discard a duplicate, giving at-most-once behavior for a retried write.

questions.prompt: Under a Lamport clock, timestamp(A) < timestamp(B) tells you...
options: if A caused B then this ordering holds, but it alone does not prove causality
questions.explanation: Lamport clocks guarantee only the forward direction; a smaller timestamp does not by itself prove a causal link.

questions.prompt: Vector clocks [2,2] and [1,3] describe events that are...
questions.explanation: Neither vector is element-wise less than or equal to the other, so the events are concurrent.

questions.prompt: A service that lets replicas converge only after writes stop provides...
questions.explanation: That is the definition of eventual consistency: convergence once writes cease, with possibly stale reads meanwhile.

questions.prompt: In a 7-node consensus cluster, the most failures it can tolerate and still make progress is...
questions.explanation: A majority of 7 is 4, so up to 3 nodes may fail while 4 remain to form a quorum.

questions.prompt: The replicated state machine approach requires that operations be...
options: deterministic and applied in identical order on every replica
questions.explanation: Identical deterministic operations in the same order keep all replicas in identical states.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, a CP system chooses to...
options: serve possibly stale data to stay available
return errors on the side it cannot safely serve, preserving consistency
questions.explanation: CP favors consistency: the minority side rejects requests rather than risk returning stale answers.

questions.prompt: Two-phase commit can leave participants blocked when...
options: the coordinator crashes after yes votes but before sending the decision
questions.explanation: Participants that voted yes hold locks and cannot safely decide alone until the coordinator recovers its decision.

questions.prompt: Partitioning writes by an ever-increasing timestamp key most likely causes...
options: a hot spot on the newest shard
questions.explanation: Every new write lands on the same newest range, overloading one shard -- a hot spot.

questions.prompt: In the fault-tolerant key-value design, what keeps a retried write from double-applying?
options: the unique request ID and server-side deduplication
questions.explanation: The state machine records applied request IDs, so a retried write is recognized and not applied twice.

questions.prompt: Why can any healthy replica of a shard answer reads correctly for that shard?
options: all replicas apply the same committed operations in the same order, so they hold identical state
questions.explanation: The replicated state machine keeps every replica identical, so any of them can serve the correct value.

lessons.title: Capstone: design your own replicated service
lessons.grammar_note: A design memo is judged on reasoning, not length: state each choice, justify it with a failure it prevents or a tradeoff it accepts, and be explicit about what your system gives up.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Design, on paper, a fault-tolerant and scalable service of your choosing -- for example a distributed counter, a URL shortener, a chat message store, or a leaderboard. Write a short design memo that makes and justifies every major decision from this course, and is honest about what the system sacrifices. Do not write code; produce the reasoning a reviewer would need to trust your design.

sections.heading: The structure to follow
sections.text: 1) State the service and its top requirement (for example, 'a URL shortener that must never lose a mapping and must scale to billions of keys'). 2) Consistency model: choose linearizable, causal, or eventual, and justify it from the requirement. 3) Replication and consensus: say how many replicas per group and how they agree (for example a 3-node Raft group), and state how many failures that tolerates. 4) Sharding: choose range or hash partitioning, name the shard key, and explain how you avoid hot spots. 5) Communication and retries: specify the delivery guarantee and how retries are made safe (request IDs or idempotency). 6) Failure handling: describe what happens when a follower crashes, when a leader crashes, and during a network partition (your CAP choice). 7) Tradeoffs: state plainly what your design gives up.

sections.heading: A fully written model (of a different service)
sections.text: Service: a distributed like-counter that must not lose likes and must scale to millions of posts. Consistency: linearizable per post, so a user who likes and refreshes always sees their like counted. Replication: each shard is a 3-node Raft group, tolerating 1 failure while keeping a majority of 2. Sharding: hash-partition by post ID across 16 shards to spread load evenly; a viral post that becomes a hot spot is given extra read replicas. Communication: writes carry a unique request ID; the state machine deduplicates, so a retried 'like' after a lost reply is counted once (at-most-once). Failure handling: a crashed follower replays the log from a snapshot to catch up; a crashed leader is replaced by a majority election among nodes with the latest log; during a partition the minority side returns errors rather than undercount -- a CP choice. Tradeoffs: during a partition the minority is unavailable, and per-post linearizability adds commit latency compared with an eventually consistent counter. Use this as a template of depth and honesty -- do not copy it; your job is the service you picked above.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: the service and its top requirement are stated before any design choices; a consistency model is named and justified from that requirement; the replication scheme states the group size and how many failures it tolerates; the sharding choice names its key and addresses hot spots; retries are made safe with request IDs or idempotency; the memo explains follower-crash, leader-crash, and partition behavior (an explicit CAP choice); and the tradeoffs section names at least one thing the system gives up. If all seven are true, you have produced a design memo that applies the whole course.
